title: Geopolitical Risks and International Business
text:
Foreword
Every multinational now says that geopolitics matters to it. Far fewer can say how much, through which channel, or what they would do differently if the number changed. The gap is not one of attention — boards discuss sanctions, export controls, wars and elections every quarter — but of measurement. Geopolitical risk reaches a firm through its market access, its inputs, its finance, its people and its data, and each of those channels can be counted. Most firms do not count them.
This book is the lecture notes of a twelve-session graduate course that tries to close that gap. Its method is simple and a little stubborn: every big idea is read, then rebuilt from its data. A landmark article or book — Caldara and Iacoviello’s geopolitical risk index, Baldwin’s Great Convergence, Kuziemko and Werker on the price of a Security Council seat, the Global Sanctions Data Base — is paired with a practice round in which the data are collected at source and its central figure is replicated in Tableau. A famous chart is a set of decisions: which countries, which years, which deflator, which coding rule. You only see the decisions when you make them yourself.
Each chapter ends on the same question: what does this figure not license a multinational to conclude? That is the habit the course is built to leave behind.

The twelve chapters




Chapter
Question




1
What is geopolitical risk?
Before we can manage geopolitical risk, what exactly are we counting?


2
The international economic order
Who wrote the rules multinationals play by — and what happens to the rules when the writers’ share of the world shrinks?


3
Anarchy and the balance of the major powers
In a system with no government above states, who sets the terms of trade — and how would a multinational know that the balance is shifting?


4
Trade, conflict and geoeconomic fragmentation
If states trade more with friends than with rivals, how does a multinational find out which side each of its markets is on — and how fast the lines are hardening?


5
International institutions
When a multinational relies on an international institution to manage its risk, is it relying on a rule — or on the states that buy and sell influence inside it?


6
Private authority, standards and global regulation
Most of the rules that govern a multinational’s daily operations were not written by a government. Who wrote them, with whose power — and does trade spread them up or down?


7
Measuring risk: content analysis, coding, big data and composite indices
Every geopolitical risk score a multinational buys or builds is a chain of choices: which texts, which words, which coder, which weights. Can you see the chain — and defend each link?


8
Cyber geopolitics and digital threats
Is cyberspace a new battlefield for great powers — or a new way for old rivals to hurt each other, with multinationals as collateral?


9
The redefinition of economic diplomacy
When states compete for markets, investment and technology, is the multinational the object of diplomacy, its instrument — or a diplomat in its own right?


10
Economic sanctions
Sanctions have become the instrument of first resort. Are they an efficient mechanism for regulating geopolitical risk — or a source of it?


11
Space geopolitics
Satellites now carry the position, timing, connectivity and imagery a multinational runs on. When orbit is crowded, contested and dominated by one operator, who holds the risk — and what can the firm do about it?


12

Can you make a board act on your assessment — and say what would change your mind?

1.2 The lecture


1.2.1 1. The course in fifteen minutes
The syllabus is SYLLABUS.md. Three things matter today:

The big theme. How does a multinational firm know how much geopolitical risk it faces — and what should it do about it?
The rhythm. Every session: a big article or book read before class; a lecture; a practice round in which you collect its data at source and rebuild its central figure in Tableau.
The grade. 80% individual. Three quizzes (Sessions 04, 07, 10), one Risk Brief (Sessions 02–11), a team dashboard for one multinational (Session 12), a 48-hour take-home.




1.2.2 2. Risk, uncertainty, and three kinds of risk
Risk versus uncertainty. Knight (1921) separated risk — outcomes whose probabilities can be estimated — from uncertainty, where they cannot. Most geopolitical events sit uncomfortably between the two: wars and coups recur, but each is unlike the last. Everything in this course is an attempt to move a question from the second category towards the first, and to be honest about how far it moves.










Question it answers
Typical unit
Example




Political risk
Can the government of the host country change the rules on me?
firm × host country
expropriation, contract renegotiation, sudden tax, licence withdrawal


Country risk
Will this country pay, convert and transfer?
country
sovereign default, capital controls, currency inconvertibility


Geopolitical risk
Will relations between states and political actors move against me?
the international system, or a dyad
war, sanctions, export controls, bloc formation, state-sponsored cyber operations



Kobrin (1979) made the classic distinction between macro risk, which hits every foreign firm in a country, and micro risk, which hits one sector or one firm. Geopolitical risk adds a third layer: risk that originates outside the host country — in Washington, Beijing, Brussels or Moscow — and reaches the firm through its suppliers, customers, banks or networks.

Family

A good risk assessment — the team project — triangulates across at least three families. The quarrel between them is informative: when the text says calm and the market says danger, someone knows something.



1.2.4 4. The GPR index: how it is built
Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) define geopolitical risk as the threat, realisation and escalation of adverse events associated with wars, terrorism and any tensions among states and political actors that affect the peaceful course of international relations.
The construction, in four steps:

Corpus. The electronic archives of ten leading newspapers (US, UK and Canadian) for the recent index from 1985; three US newspapers for the historical index from 1900.
Dictionary. Articles are counted if they contain words from eight categories — war threats, peace threats, military build-ups, nuclear threats, terror threats, beginning of war, escalation of war, terror acts — usually in combination with words that pin the article to geopolitics.
Share. For each month, the number of GPR articles divided by the total number of articles. Dividing by the total removes the effect of newspapers growing or shrinking.
Normalisation. The share is rescaled so that the 1985–2019 average equals 100.

Threats versus acts. The first five categories form GPR Threats, the last three GPR Acts. The distinction matters to a firm: the paper finds that threats, not only realised acts, depress investment.
Validation. The authors audit samples of articles by hand, compare the index with historical narrative, and show it spikes at the events it should — the World Wars, Korea, the Cuban missile crisis, the Gulf War, 9/11, the 2003 invasion of Iraq, the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Country-specific indices. For several dozen countries, the same counts are restricted to articles that also mention the country — a measure of how much the anglophone press associates that country with geopolitical tension.



1.2.5 5. Why a firm should care
The real-options channel. When an investment is costly to reverse and the future is uncertain, waiting has value (Bernanke, 1983; Bloom, 2009). A GPR spike raises the value of waiting: firms postpone hiring, capital expenditure and entry. Caldara and Iacoviello find that higher GPR predicts lower investment and employment, and that the effect is stronger in industries more exposed to geopolitical risk.

1.2.6 6. What GPR does not tell you

It measures attention in the anglophone press, not the risk faced by a subsidiary in Abidjan or a supplier in Shenzhen.
It is global: one number for the world. The country indices help, but only for countries the newspapers write about.
Attention fades even while risk persists: a frozen conflict may be a constant risk and a falling index.
It is not a forecast. It rises with an event; it does not tell you the next one.

That list is the template for “the catch” — the last step of every practice round.

title: 2  The international economic order
text:
2.2 The lecture
The session opens with four Risk Briefs (20 minutes); the lecture takes the next seventy.


2.2.1 1. What an “economic order” is
An international order is a set of rules, institutions and expectations that governs relations between states, backed by some distribution of power. An economic order is the part of it that governs trade, money and investment — the part a multinational lives inside without noticing, until it changes.
Three questions describe any economic order:







Question
What to look at




Who wrote the rules?
Which states designed the institutions, and in whose interest


What do the rules say?
Openness to trade, to capital, to investment; how disputes are settled


What holds them in place?
Hegemonic power, shared interest, institutions with their own momentum






2.2.2 2. The post-1945 order, in four layers
Bretton Woods (1944). Forty-four allied states create the International Monetary Fund (stable exchange rates, balance-of-payments support) and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the core of the World Bank. Fixed but adjustable exchange rates anchored on the dollar, the dollar on gold.
The GATT (1947). A provisional agreement — the planned International Trade Organization never came into being — that cuts tariffs in successive rounds on the principle of most-favoured-nation treatment and national treatment.
Embedded liberalism. Ruggie (1982) named the bargain: openness abroad, made politically sustainable by social protection and macroeconomic autonomy at home. Capital controls were normal; free trade was managed.
The neoliberal turn and the WTO (1995). The dollar’s link to gold ends in 1971; capital controls are dismantled through the 1980s and 1990s; the Uruguay Round creates the World Trade Organization, with a binding dispute-settlement mechanism and rules reaching into services, intellectual property (TRIPS) and investment measures (TRIMs). China joins in 2001.
The liberal order as a political project. Ikenberry (2011, Liberal Leviathan) argues the order was American-led but easy to join and hard to overturn: open, rule-based, institutional enough that rising states gain more by joining than by challenging it. Session 03 sets the realist reply beside it.



2.2.3 3. Baldwin’s three unbundlings
Baldwin organises globalisation around three costs: of moving goods, moving ideas, and moving people.









Phase
What became cheap
What it unbundled
Consequence




First unbundling (steam, from the 19th century)
moving goods
production from consumption: you could make things far from where they were bought
Industry clustered in the North, where ideas stayed cheap to move locally. Great divergence between North and South


Second unbundling (ICT, from about 1990)
moving ideas
the factory itself: stages of production could be offshored while coordinated from headquarters
Northern know-how moved South inside the multinational’s value chain. Great convergence


Third unbundling (prospective)
moving people — virtually: telepresence, telerobotics
the worker from the workplace
Services trade in tasks; competition reaches occupations, not only sectors



The key point for this course. In the second unbundling, the multinational is the vehicle of convergence. Know-how is transferred through supply chains the firm controls. That is why geopolitics now reaches firms so directly: the supply chain is where technology, jobs and security dependence travel together.
Baldwin’s evidence is a picture: the G7’s share of world income, rising for over a century, then falling sharply after about 1990 — while a handful of developing economies (his “Industrialising Six”: China, Korea, India, Poland, Indonesia, Thailand) gain almost all of it. That is today’s target figure.



2.2.4 4. From convergence to backlash
Rodrik’s trilemma (Rodrik, 2011, The Globalization Paradox): a country can have at most two of deep economic integration, national sovereignty and democratic politics.








Choose
Give up
Looks like




integration + sovereignty
democracy
the “golden straitjacket”: policies dictated by markets


integration + democracy
sovereignty
global federalism: rules made above the state


sovereignty + democracy
deep integration
Bretton Woods compromise: shallow, managed openness



The trilemma reads the 2010s and 2020s: Brexit, tariff wars, industrial policy, export controls, and “de-risking” are choices of sovereignty and democracy over integration.
Slowbalisation. World trade in percent of GDP rose steeply from the 1990s to 2008 and has broadly flattened since. Whether that is a retreat from globalisation or a shift in its form — from goods to services and data — is contested. The extend step of the practice round lets you see the flattening and judge it.
When the writers’ share shrinks. If the G7 produced around two-thirds of world GDP when it wrote the rules, and much less today, two questions follow — and they open Sessions 03 and 04: will the rules be rewritten by the new powers (power transition), and will the world split into blocs with rules of their own (fragmentation)?



2.2.5 5. What it means for the multinational







Implication
Example




Your market is no longer where the rules are written.
A European firm earns a growing share of revenue in markets whose governments did not design the WTO and do not feel bound by its spirit


Your supply chain is a geopolitical object.
The know-how the second unbundling moved is what export controls now try to stop


Multilateral protection is weaker.
The WTO’s Appellate Body has been unable to hear appeals since December 2019; disputes are settled by power more often than by panels


Measurement choices are strategy choices.
At market exchange rates, the G7 still looks large; at PPP, it looks much smaller. Which one a board sees shapes where it builds






2.2.6 6. What the figure does not license

A falling G7 share is relative: G7 economies kept growing. It does not mean the G7 market shrank.
At current US dollars, the share moves with the dollar: part of any year-to-year change is the exchange rate, not production.
Convergence is concentrated. Most of the gain goes to a handful of countries — above all China. “The South” did not converge.
It shows income, not rule-making power. Whether shrinking share means shrinking influence is the question of Session 03, not a reading of this chart.




2.2.7 7. The Tableau skill of the day
DataBank gives you years as columns. Tableau wants one row per country-year. Select the year columns in the data source pane → right-click → Pivot. Rename Pivot Field Names to Year and Pivot Field Values to Value. Change Year to a number or date and Value to a number — DataBank’s .. become nulls. Then build the G7 share with a calculated field, and check it with a percent of total table calculation. Full click-path: ../02-practice/README.md.

title: 3  Anarchy and the balance of the major powers
text:
3.2 The lecture
The session opens with four Risk Briefs (20 minutes); the lecture takes the next seventy.


3.2.1 1. Anarchy: the starting point
In international relations, anarchy means the absence of a government above states — no world authority that can make rules binding, enforce contracts or guarantee survival. It does not mean chaos or constant war: most of the time, most states are at peace and trade under rules.
What follows from anarchy, in the realist tradition:

Self-help. Each state must ultimately ensure its own survival.
Uncertainty about intentions. A state cannot know what another will do with its power tomorrow.
Relative gains. Because today’s partner may be tomorrow’s adversary, states care not only what they gain from cooperation but how much more the other gains (Grieco, 1988).

Why a firm should care. Relative-gains thinking is why trade becomes a security question: a deal that makes both richer but the rival richer faster may be refused, restricted or reversed. It is the logic behind export controls on advanced semiconductors.



3.2.2 2. Two realisms
Defensive realism — Waltz (1979), Theory of International Politics. The structure of the system — anarchy plus the distribution of capabilities — shapes behaviour. States seek an appropriate amount of power: enough for security. Too much provokes balancing coalitions, so expansion is usually self-defeating. Waltz judged bipolar systems more stable than multipolar ones: fewer miscalculations.
The security dilemma (Jervis, 1978). What one state does to make itself secure — arming, alliances — makes others less secure, and they respond. Both end up worse off without anyone intending aggression.
Offensive realism — Mearsheimer (2001). Five bedrock assumptions:

The international system is anarchic.
Great powers possess some offensive military capability.
States can never be certain of others’ intentions.
Survival is the primary goal of great powers.
Great powers are rational actors.

From these, Mearsheimer derives that great powers maximise relative power; the ideal is to be the regional hegemon and to prevent any other region from having one. His prediction for China: it will try to dominate Asia as the United States dominates the Western Hemisphere, and the United States will try to stop it. “China cannot rise peacefully.”









Defensive (Waltz)
Offensive (Mearsheimer)




How much power do states want?
enough for security
as much as possible, relative to others


What restrains them?
balancing by others
only the limits of their capabilities


Expected US–China outcome
managed competition
intense security competition






3.2.3 3. Power transition and the Thucydides’s Trap
Power transition theory (Organski, 1958; Organski & Kugler, 1980) reverses Waltz’s emphasis: hierarchy, not balance, keeps the peace. A dominant power sets the international order. War is most likely when a dissatisfied challenger approaches parity with the dominant power — a threshold often operationalised as the challenger reaching around 80% of the leader’s capabilities.
Allison (2017). “It was the rise of Athens and the fear that this instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable” (Thucydides). Allison and the Harvard Thucydides’s Trap project identify sixteen cases in five hundred years in which a rising power challenged a ruling one; twelve ended in war.
The critics.

Case selection. The cases are chosen on the outcome of interest; peaceful transitions (the UK to the US) may be under-counted; the definition of “rising” and “ruling” is elastic.
Nuclear weapons change the expected cost of great-power war in a way no pre-1945 case can capture.
Interdependence. The US and China are bound by trade and finance far more tightly than Athens and Sparta, or Britain and Germany — though Britain and Germany were also major trading partners in 1914 (Session 04 takes this up).
Measuring “rise”. Beckley (2018) argues gross indicators — GDP, population, CINC — overstate China’s power because they ignore the costs of governing, feeding and protecting a population.




3.2.4 4. Measuring power: the CINC
The Correlates of War Composite Index of National Capability (Singer, Bremer & Stuckey, 1972):

Take six indicators for every state in the system each year: total population, urban population, iron and steel production, primary energy consumption, military personnel, military expenditure.
For each indicator, compute the state’s share of the system total that year.
Average the six shares. CINC is a number between 0 and 1; the system sums to about 1 (not exactly: a state missing a component is averaged over the ones it has).

What it rewards. Size and heavy industry. Two of six components are population and two are smokestack industry. CINC therefore shows China passing the United States much earlier than military spending or GDP at market exchange rates do. One reality, three measures, three dates: the break step of the practice round is to see it.
What it misses. Technology, quality of forces, alliances, financial power, control of networks — the dollar, SWIFT, the cloud — which Session 08 and Session 11 show to be the instruments of coercion that reach firms most directly.



3.2.5 5. What it means for the multinational







The balance of power sets the rules of trade
Who can impose sanctions, export controls and market-access conditions depends on who holds capabilities others need


A transition changes which rules you follow
A firm in both the US and China increasingly faces two compliance regimes — and penalties for following one in the other’s jurisdiction


Relative gains turn commerce into security
Products that make a rival stronger — chips, AI, batteries, aerospace — move from the trade ministry to the security council


The date of the transition depends on the measure
Board slides that say “China has overtaken the US” should say on what


Security dilemmas escalate without intent
A defensive move by one side (an export control, a military exercise) is read as offensive and triggers a response that reaches your supply chain






3.2.6 6. What the figure does not license

CINC is a measure of material capabilities, not of influence, intentions or likelihood of war. A crossover on the chart is not a prediction of conflict.
It overweights size: population and heavy industry. It cannot see semiconductors, alliances or finance.
It ends in 2022: the most recent shifts are not in it.
It describes states, not markets: a firm’s exposure depends on where its revenue and suppliers sit, not on the system’s distribution of power.




3.2.7 7. The Tableau skill of the day
Calculated fields to build a ratio (challenger CINC ÷ US CINC), a parameter so the viewer can choose the challenger, a reference line at parity and at the 80% threshold, and a dual axis to set CINC against military spending. Click-path: ../02-practice/README.md.

Allison, G. (2017). Destined for war: Can America and China escape Thucydides’s trap? Houghton Mifflin Harcourt.
Beckley, M. (2018). The power of nations: Measuring what matters. International Security, 43(2), 7–44.
Grieco, J. M. (1988). Anarchy and the limits of cooperation: A realist critique of the newest liberal institutionalism. International Organization, 42(3), 485–507.
Jervis, R. (1978). Cooperation under the security dilemma. World Politics, 30(2), 167–214.
Mearsheimer, J. J. (2001). The tragedy of great power politics. W. W. Norton.
Organski, A. F. K. (1958). World politics. Knopf.

Singer, J. D., Bremer, S., & Stuckey, J. (1972). Capability distribution, uncertainty, and major power war, 1820–1965. In B. Russett (Ed.), Peace, war, and numbers (pp. 19–48). Sage.
Waltz, K. N. (1979). Theory of international politics. Addison-Wesley.

title: 4  Trade, conflict and geoeconomic fragmentation
text:
4.2 The lecture
The session opens with Quiz 1 (20 minutes) and four Risk Briefs (20 minutes); the lecture takes the remaining fifty.


4.2.1 1. Does trade keep the peace? The liberal answer
The commercial peace is one of the oldest ideas in international political economy. From Montesquieu (“peace is the natural effect of trade”) to Norman Angell’s The Great Illusion (1910), the argument is that trade raises the opportunity cost of war: states that gain from exchange lose those gains if they fight.
Modern versions add mechanisms:

Opportunity cost. Conflict disrupts trade; the more a dyad trades, the more it loses.
Signalling. Interdependent states can send costly signals — threatening economic ties — short of force, which reduces miscalculation.
Domestic coalitions. Trade creates exporters and importers with a stake in peaceful relations who lobby their governments.
Institutions. Trade agreements create forums and dispute-settlement procedures.

Statistical studies of dyads from the 1990s onwards (notably Russett & Oneal’s Triangulating Peace, 2001) found that dyads with more trade relative to GDP experience fewer militarised disputes.



4.2.2 2. The realist critique
Realists reply that interdependence can cause conflict:

Vulnerability. Dependence on a rival for essential goods is a security risk. States therefore limit it — or fight to secure supplies (Waltz, 1979).
Relative gains (Session 03). If trade makes the rival stronger faster, it is a threat.
Security externalities (Gowa, 1994). Trade raises the economic capacity of the partner; states therefore trade more with allies than with adversaries.
Expectations of future trade (Copeland, 2015). What matters is not today’s trade but whether leaders expect it to continue. When they expect to be cut off, interdependence becomes a reason to act before the window closes.

The history the realists point to: Britain and Germany were heavily interdependent in 1914.



4.2.3 3. What the evidence says: Mansfield (2021)
Mansfield’s review in the Oxford Handbook of International Political Economy sets out the debate and the main empirical findings. Four points to retain:

The relationship runs both ways. Conflict reduces trade, so a negative correlation between trade and conflict does not by itself show that trade causes peace.
Institutions matter. Preferential trading arrangements are associated with fewer disputes among members (Mansfield & Pevehouse, 2000).
Context matters. The effect differs with regime type, the level of development, and the distribution of power between the partners.
The question has changed. As geopolitical competition returned, research has turned from “does trade pacify?” to “how do states use trade as an instrument of conflict?” — the questions of Sessions 08, 10 and 11.




4.2.4 4. Bilateral versus multilateral openness
Martin, Mayer & Thoenig (2008), Make Trade Not War?, Review of Economic Studies, 75(3), 865–900 (doi:10.1111/j.1467-937X.2008.00492.x).
Their argument separates two effects:








Effect on the risk of a bilateral conflict




Bilateral trade between A and B
lowers it: A and B have more to lose from fighting each other


Multilateral trade openness of A and B with the rest of the world
raises it: if A can trade with everyone else, losing B costs less



The implication is uncomfortable for the liberal view: globalisation lowers the cost of bilateral conflict because it provides substitutes. A world of many alternative suppliers makes it cheaper to break with any one of them. Their empirical work finds support for both effects.



4.2.5 5. Fragmentation: the new question
Friend-shoring (a term popularised in US policy debate in 2022) proposes to move supply chains towards trusted partners. De-risking (the European Commission’s term, 2023) proposes to reduce dependence on rivals in critical goods without breaking trade overall. De-coupling is the end point: separate economic blocs.
Gopinath, Gourinchas, Presbitero & Topalova (2025) ask whether the data show this happening. Their design:

Define blocs. Countries are grouped into a US-leaning bloc, a China-leaning bloc and a non-aligned group on the basis of their foreign-policy alignment as revealed by UN General Assembly voting. Read Section 2 of the paper for exactly which vote or measure, and which year, they use — ours will be a simplification, and you must say how it differs.
Compare trade within and between blocs before and after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, controlling for the usual determinants of bilateral trade.
Look for connectors — non-aligned countries whose trade with both blocs grew, through which some between-bloc trade may be rerouted.

Their main finding: after the invasion, trade between the two blocs fell relative to trade within them, by a margin of the order of ten percent or more (find the exact estimate in the paper and write it in your notes), and foreign direct investment shows a similar pattern. They are careful to say this is a fragmentation still small compared with the Cold War — but it is happening, and it is concentrated in strategic sectors.



4.2.6 6. What it means for the multinational







Classify your markets by alignment
Which of your five most important countries (the team milestone) sit in which bloc — and which are drifting?


Connectors are opportunities and risks
Mexico, Vietnam and others gain between-bloc trade — and attract scrutiny for transshipment and rules-of-origin enforcement


The cost of switching is falling for states, not for you
Martin, Mayer & Thoenig: multilateral openness makes it cheaper for states to break with a partner. Your supply contracts do not get cheaper to break


De-risking is sectoral
Fragmentation is concentrated in strategic goods; a firm in consumer goods and one in semiconductors face different worlds






4.2.7 7. What the figure does not license

A fall in between-bloc trade is a correlation with a date, not proof that geopolitics caused it: sanctions on Russia, the post-COVID rebound and price changes all move trade values in the same years.
Bloc membership is a modelling choice. Change the threshold or the base year and countries move between blocs — and the figure moves with them.
Values, not volumes. Trade in US dollars rises with commodity prices; 2022 was a year of very high energy and food prices.
It shows aggregate trade. Your firm’s products may be in a sector where fragmentation is far stronger — or absent.




4.2.8 8. The Tableau skill of the day
A dyadic table (exporter × partner × year) needs two copies of the country table: one for the exporter’s bloc, one for the partner’s. In Tableau’s data model, add the bloc table, relate it on exporter = country, then add it again and relate the second copy on partner = country. Blocs are sets defined by a condition on the ideal point, with parameters as thresholds. The trade series is indexed to a base year with a table calculation. Click-path: ../02-practice/README.md.

The target. Gopinath, Gourinchas, Presbitero & Topalova (2025): trade between geopolitical blocs against trade within them, before and after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Work in your team. One extract per team; everyone builds their own workbook.


4.3.1 1 · Collect — 10 min
Ideal points and codebook from Dataverse; your IMF IMTS extract of bilateral goods exports, annual, 2015–latest. If not done: ../data/README.md.
Provenance log: one line per file. For the ideal points, log version 39 and the change to calendar-year estimation. For IMF, log the date of the extract and the exact indicator you chose.



4.3.2 2 · Prepare — 25 min

4.3.2.1 A · Classify countries into blocs (ideal points)

Connect → Text file → IdealpointestimatesFP_2026FP.csv. The ISO 3-letter code, the year and the ideal point are iso3c, year and IdealPointFP (see the codebook). Rename iso3c → iso3 and IdealPointFP → IdealPoint (right-click → Rename): the steps below use those names.
New sheet. Filter year = 2021 — the last full year before the invasion. (Gopinath et al. may use a different reference: check, and log the difference.)
Read the ideal points of the US (USA) and China (CHN) off the data. Create two parameters, US ref and CHN ref (Float), and type those two values in.
Create a third parameter Margin (Float, start at 0.5) and the calculated field:
Bloc =
IF ABS([IdealPoint] - [CHN ref]) - ABS([IdealPoint] - [US ref]) > [Margin] THEN "US-leaning"
ELSEIF ABS([IdealPoint] - [US ref]) - ABS([IdealPoint] - [CHN ref]) > [Margin] THEN "China-leaning"
ELSE "Non-aligned"
END
iso3 → Rows, Bloc → Rows, IdealPoint → Text. Sort by ideal point. Does the classification look right for countries you know? Adjust Margin until you can defend it — and write down the value and why.
Export the classification as a derived file: Worksheet → Export → Crosstab to Excel (or View Data → Export All to CSV). Save it as data/derived/blocs_2021.csv — not in raw/. Add a provenance line: derived from the ideal points, Margin = …, base year 2021.



4.3.2.2 B · Relate trade to blocs — the dyad model

New data source: Connect → Text file (or Excel) → your IMF extract. Identify the exporter, partner, year and value columns — in the IMF’s SDMX layout COUNTRY, COUNTERPART_COUNTRY, TIME_PERIOD, OBS_VALUE — and rename them exporter, partner, year, value. Keep only INDICATOR = XG_FOB_USD.
Remove aggregate partners (“World”, “Advanced Economies”, regions — codes starting with G or TX, e.g. G001 World): filter them out, and log which.
In the data source pane, drag blocs_2021.csv onto the canvas: Tableau creates a relationship. Click the noodle → relate exporter = iso3.
Drag blocs_2021.csv onto the canvas a second time. Relate partner = iso3. Rename this copy Partner blocs and its Bloc field Partner bloc; rename the first copy’s field Exporter bloc.
IMTS uses ISO3 codes, so the relationship works directly. If your download shows names instead, you need a concordance table — log it.





4.3.3 3 · Replicate — 25 min

4.3.3.1 Sheet 1 · “Trade within and between blocs”

The pair type:
Pair type =
IF [Exporter bloc] = "Non-aligned" OR [Partner bloc] = "Non-aligned" THEN "Involves non-aligned"
ELSEIF [Exporter bloc] = [Partner bloc] THEN "Within bloc"
ELSE "Between US- and China-leaning"
END
The index, 2021 = 100:
Trade index = SUM([value]) / WINDOW_SUM(SUM(IF [year] = 2021 THEN [value] END)) * 100
year → Columns as a discrete dimension (blue); Trade index → Rows; Pair type → Colour. Right-click Trade index → Edit Table Calculation → Compute Using → year, so each pair type is indexed to its own 2021.
Reference line at 100. Annotate 2022.
Title with the finding. Caption: both sources with versions, and “Blocs: ideal-point distance to US vs China, 2021, margin = …”.



4.3.3.2 Sheet 2 · “Who sits where?” — the classification on a map
iso3 (geographic role Country/Region, ISO 3166-1 alpha-3) on the map, coloured by Bloc. Mark your team firm’s five main countries with a group (Create → Group, “Our markets”).




4.3.4 4 · Compare and break — 20 min

Compare. Put Sheet 1 beside the paper’s figure. Their data are quarterly and their estimate controls for other determinants of trade; ours is annual and raw. Does the direction match? Is the gap between “within” and “between” of a similar order? Write one difference and its likely cause.
Break the bloc definition. Move Margin (0.25, 1.0), re-export, refresh. Which countries change bloc? Does the gap between the lines survive? This is the most important answer of the round.
Break the side of the trade. If your extract has the mirror series (imports reported by the partner), rebuild the index with it. Same picture?
Extend — connectors. Create a set of non-aligned countries (Create → Set, Top tab: top 10 by growth in exports to both blocs, 2021 → latest — or pick by hand from a table). Which are they? Is any of them among your firm’s markets?

title: 5  International institutions
text:
5.2 The lecture


5.2.1 1. Why would states under anarchy build institutions at all?
Session 03 left us with a system without a government above states. Session 04 showed trade reorganising itself along geopolitical lines. Yet the same system is dense with institutions — the UN, the WTO, the IMF, the World Bank, investment treaties, export-control regimes. Why?









Liberal institutionalism
Realism




Key text
Keohane (1984), After Hegemony
Mearsheimer (1994/95), The False Promise of International Institutions


Why institutions exist
They lower the transaction costs of cooperation, provide information, and lengthen the shadow of the future so that states can make credible commitments
They reflect the distribution of power; the strong build them to serve their interests


Do they constrain states?
Yes, at the margin — states comply because the institution makes reneging costly and cooperation valuable
Rarely — when interests and rules collide, power wins


What it predicts for a firm
Rules are a reasonably stable floor: dispute settlement, treaties, sanctions regimes behave predictably
Rules are only as stable as the coalition behind them; read the coalition, not the treaty



Neither is a strawman. The useful question for a firm is not which theory is “true” but which institution, on which issue, behaves like which. That is an empirical question — and Kuziemko and Werker give one of its sharpest answers.



5.2.2 2. The Security Council in five facts

Fifteen members: five permanent (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States) and ten elected. Before 1966 there were six elected members.
Elected members serve two-year terms, five elected each year by the General Assembly, by regional group, with a two-thirds majority; they cannot be immediately re-elected.
Decisions on substantive matters need nine votes and no veto from a permanent member.
Under Chapter VII the Council can impose measures — sanctions, arms embargoes, the use of force — that bind every UN member state.
An elected member’s vote can be pivotal: the P5 need nine votes, so they must court elected members.




5.2.3 3. The price of a seat — Kuziemko and Werker (2006)
The question. Do powerful states pay for the votes of elected Security Council members?
The identification idea. Countries do not choose when they rotate onto the Council in any way that tracks their need for aid — rotation follows regional queues and norms. So the authors compare a country with itself in the years before, during and after its term. If aid rises during the term and falls back afterwards, the seat — not the country’s poverty, alliances or politics — is the likeliest explanation.
The findings, in the paper’s own summary:

US aid to a developing country rises substantially — by about 59% in the abstract’s headline estimate — when it rotates onto the Council, and aid through the UN rises too, more modestly.
The increase is concentrated in the term years and disappears after the term.
The effect is larger in years when the Council matters more — measured by how much the press covered it.

Why that last result matters. It is the difference between a statistical curiosity and a mechanism. If aid followed membership whatever the Council was doing, rotation might proxy for something else. That aid tracks the salience of Council business is what makes “vote buying” the most plausible reading.
The follow-up literature. Dreher, Sturm and Vreeland extended the question to the World Bank and the IMF, and Vreeland and Dreher (2014), The Political Economy of the United Nations Security Council: Money and Influence (Cambridge University Press), brings the evidence together. The common thread: temporary members of the Council receive more favourable treatment in several channels.



5.2.4 4. What it means for multinational firms
Institutions enter a firm’s risk in at least four places:









Where
Institution
What the firm relies on
What Kuziemko and Werker warn




Sanctions
UN Security Council (Chapter VII); then national and EU regimes (Session 10)
A predictable list of who is sanctioned and why
Resolutions are bargained; votes have prices; a P5 veto blocks UN sanctions — and pushes them into unilateral national regimes that diverge


Investment protection
Bilateral investment treaties; ICSID arbitration
A neutral forum if a host state expropriates
Treaties are only as strong as the host state’s willingness to pay awards


Political risk insurance
MIGA (World Bank Group), national export-credit agencies
Cover against expropriation, war, transfer restrictions
The insurer’s own shareholders are states — cover is a political decision too


Trade rules
WTO dispute settlement
Tariff bindings, non-discrimination
The Appellate Body has been unable to function since 2019; “rules” now depend on the coalition



The lesson for the firm. An international institution is a risk mitigator when the coalition that sustains it is stable, and a risk source when it is not. A risk dashboard should therefore track not only the rules but the coalition: who sits on the Council, how they vote, what they are being offered — which is exactly what today’s practice round builds.



5.2.5 5. The Tableau skill of the day — LOD expressions
The practice needs two numbers for every country-year that do not exist in either file:
Years relative to a term. Join the term table (one row per term) to the aid table (one row per country-year) on the country code — a join in the physical layer, not a relationship, because a row-level calculation cannot mix fields from two related tables. Each country-year now appears once per term of that country, which is exactly what an event study needs:
[Event time]   =  [Year] - [Term start]
The country’s own pre-term baseline, a Level of Detail expression that fixes the computation at the country × term level whatever is in the view:
[Baseline aid] = { FIXED [Iso3], [Term start] :
                   AVG( IF [Event time] >= -3 AND [Event time] <= -1 THEN [Aid] END ) }

[Aid relative to baseline] = [Aid] / [Baseline aid]      // row level: one value per country-year-term
FIXED computes before the view’s dimension filters (context filters apply first) and ignores what is on Rows and Columns: every row of a term carries that term’s baseline. The ratio is then computed row by row, and averaging it at each event year gives the average across terms of a ratio computed within each term.

Kuziemko, I., & Werker, E. (2006). How much is a seat on the Security Council worth? Foreign aid and bribery at the United Nations. Journal of Political Economy, 114(5), 905–930. https://doi.org/10.1086/507155

title: 6  Private authority, standards and global regulation
text:
6.2 The lecture


6.2.1 1. The rules a firm actually follows
Session 05 looked at intergovernmental institutions. But walk through a multinational’s supply chain and count the rules it obeys: quality management (ISO 9001), environmental management (ISO 14001), information security (ISO/IEC 27001), forest and fisheries certification, labour codes of conduct, carbon accounting (the GHG Protocol), sustainability reporting standards, telecom technical specifications. Most were not written by a government. They are written by private or hybrid bodies, adopted voluntarily — and then made compulsory by buyers, investors and export markets.
That is private authority: the capacity of non-state actors to make rules that others treat as binding. For a multinational it is both a risk (a standard written elsewhere becomes a condition of market access) and a lever (a firm that shapes the standard shapes the market).



6.2.2 2. The governance triangle — Abbott and Snidal (2009)
Abbott and Snidal map regulatory standards-setting (RSS) schemes in a triangle whose corners are the three types of actor that can write rules:
                       STATE
                        /\
                       /  \
                      /    \
                     /      \
                    /        \
                   /__________\
                FIRM           NGO

Schemes near a corner are run by one actor type: an industry code of conduct (firms), an activist certification (NGOs), an intergovernmental rule (states).
Schemes in the middle are hybrids: firms and NGOs together (multi-stakeholder certification); states, firms and NGOs together (the UN Global Compact is often placed here).
The shadow of the state: even private schemes are shaped by the possibility that states will regulate if private actors do not — and by states choosing to endorse, require or ignore them.

Why it matters for a firm. Where a scheme sits predicts how it behaves: who can change it, how legitimate NGOs and governments will find it, and whether a state may one day make it mandatory.



6.2.3 3. Standards and power — Mattli and Büthe (2003)
Who wins when an international product standard is written at ISO or the IEC? Mattli and Büthe compare three explanations:







Explanation
Prediction




Technological rationality
The technically best solution wins, whoever proposes it


Primacy of power
The standard favours the states with the largest markets


Institutional complementarity (their argument)
Countries whose domestic standard-setting system is hierarchical and coordinated — matching the structure of ISO/IEC — are more effective at shaping international standards than countries with fragmented domestic systems



Their evidence points to institutional complementarity: the coordinated European national standards bodies were better placed than the fragmented, decentralised US system. The lesson: influence over “technical” rules depends on how a country — and its firms — are organised to take part.
Today, that is geopolitics. The competition over telecommunications standards, over battery and charging standards, over AI and data rules, is a competition between blocs, each trying to make its domestic rules the world’s. Bradford’s Brussels effect (2020) describes how EU rules become global because firms find it cheaper to adopt the strictest rule everywhere than to run two production lines.



6.2.4 4. Three perspectives on standardization — Brunsson, Rasche and Seidl (2012)
Brunsson and colleagues organise research on standards around three aspects:

standardization of organizations — standards that tell firms how to be organised (management system standards such as ISO 14001);
standardization by organizations — the bodies that write standards and how they work;
standardization as organization — standards as a way of organising markets and fields without formal hierarchy.

Their key point is that standards, usually associated with stability and sameness, are dynamic: they are revised, contested, translated locally, decoupled from practice. A firm “certified” to ISO 14001 may run its plants exactly as before — the certificate and the practice can diverge.



6.2.5 5. Delegated or entrepreneurial — Green (2013)
Green distinguishes two sources of private authority:









Delegated
Entrepreneurial




Origin
States hand rule-making to private actors
Private actors create rules on their own, and others adopt them


Illustration (carbon governance, Green’s field)
Private bodies accrediting and verifying projects under the Kyoto Protocol’s Clean Development Mechanism
Voluntary carbon accounting and offset standards, such as the GHG Protocol


What a firm should watch
The state that delegated can take it back
Adoption — the rule is as strong as the number of users






6.2.6 6. Race to the bottom, or trading up? — Prakash and Potoski (2006)
The worry. Trade intensifies competition; governments lower environmental standards to attract investment and win exports — a race to the bottom.
The alternative. Vogel’s (1995) California effect: exporters to strict markets adopt strict standards, and trade spreads them — trading up.
The test. ISO 14001 is a voluntary environmental management standard that goes beyond what many domestic laws require. Prakash and Potoski use a panel of 108 countries over seven years and ask whether adoption in a country depends on adoption in its export markets.
The finding. Trade linkages encourage ISO 14001 adoption when a country’s major export markets have themselves adopted it. Trade spreads private standards upward — towards the standards of the customers.
For the firm. A private standard can become a de facto condition of access to a market without a single law changing. Monitoring “regulatory” risk means monitoring what your customers’ home markets adopt.



6.2.7 7. The Tableau skill of the day — maps and Pages

Give iso3 the geographic role Country/Region (right-click → Geographic Role). Tableau recognises ISO 3166 codes; check the “unknown” indicator at the bottom right of the map and fix what it could not place (Map → Edit Locations).
Filled map of certificates per billion US$ of GDP; colour on a sequential palette, never a rainbow.
Year on the Pages shelf: a play button animates the diffusion.
Small multiples: Region on Rows and Year on Columns with a line of the median country — the same story, without animation, on one page.

7.2 The lecture


7.2.1 1. The measurement chain
Every number in this course — GPR, a capability share, an ideal point, a sanctions count — is the end of a chain:
concept  →  indicator  →  source  →  coding rule  →  aggregation  →  presentation
"geopolitical    "share of      ten          the eight       monthly share,    a line with
 risk"           articles…"     newspapers   categories      base 1985–2019    spikes labelled
Two questions apply to every link:

Validity — does the indicator measure the concept? (Is newspaper attention geopolitical risk?)
Reliability — would someone else, following the same rules, get the same number? (Would a second coder put the same article in the same category?)

A measure can be perfectly reliable and invalid — a thermometer read identically by everyone that measures the wrong room. Today is about seeing every link, so you can audit a score you are sold and defend one you build.



7.2.2 2. Content analysis
Krippendorff (2018) defines content analysis as a research technique for making replicable and valid inferences from texts to the contexts of their use. Its steps:








Step
In the GPR index
In your coding today




Unitising — what is one unit?
an article
a headline


Sampling — which units?
all articles in ten newspapers
40 headlines drawn at random from a GDELT query


Recording / coding — which category?
a dictionary of words
two human coders and a protocol


Reducing — how are codes summarised?
monthly share
counts and shares by category


Inferring — what do we conclude?
geopolitical risk is high
your firm’s countries are in the news for …



Manifest vs latent content. A dictionary sees manifest content — the words on the page. Human coders can see latent content — what an article is about. Dictionaries are cheap, fast and perfectly reliable; humans are slow and less reliable but can catch meaning. The best measures use both: a dictionary, audited by humans.



7.2.3 3. Three dictionary methods










GPR — Caldara & Iacoviello
EPU — Baker, Bloom & Davis
PRisk — Hassan et al.




Text
newspaper articles

learned: bigrams frequent in political texts and rare in non-political ones


Scaled by
all articles
all articles

Level

Validation
narrative, hand audit

What Hassan et al. add. Political risk becomes a firm-level variable — measured from what managers and analysts actually discuss. Their striking finding is that most of the variation in political risk is across firms at a given time, not common to all firms: aggregate indices like EPU, however useful, miss most of the political risk an individual firm faces.



7.2.4 4. Reliability: how much do coders agree?
Percent agreement — the share of items both coders put in the same category — is intuitive and misleading: two coders guessing at random will often agree, especially when one category dominates.
Cohen’s kappa corrects for chance:
\[
\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}
\qquad
p_o = \frac{\text{agreements}}{N}
\qquad
p_e = \sum_k \frac{n_{A,k}}{N}\cdot\frac{n_{B,k}}{N}
\]
where \(n_{A,k}\) is the number of items coder A put in category \(k\).
A worked example. 40 headlines, three collapsed categories: not geopolitical (0), threat (1–5), act (6–8).

\(p_o = (20 + 8 + 5)/40 = 0.825\)
\(p_e = (24\cdot22 + 10\cdot12 + 6\cdot6)/40^2 = 684/1600 = 0.4275\)
\(\kappa = (0.825 - 0.4275)/(1 - 0.4275) \approx 0.69\)

An 82.5% agreement becomes a kappa of about 0.69 once chance is removed. Conventions differ: Landis and Koch’s widely used labels call 0.61–0.80 “substantial”; Krippendorff, for his alpha (the generalisation to more coders, missing data and other scales), asks for at least 0.800 for firm conclusions and accepts 0.667 only for tentative ones.
What to do with disagreement. Never average it away. Read each disagreement, decide whether the protocol was unclear or a coder erred, revise the protocol, and adjudicate. The disagreements are where the concept is fuzzy — they are information.



7.2.5 5. Big data: what it adds, what it hides
GDELT monitors news in many languages worldwide and turns it into searchable records. Its promise is coverage and speed: every country, every day, without a research assistant.
Its traps:

Selection. Only what is reported, by sources GDELT monitors, in languages it processes. Coverage changes over time: a rising count may be more sources, not more events.
Duplication. One wire story becomes hundreds of articles.
Machine coding. Automated event coding misreads irony, quotation, and historical references.
“N = all” is never all. A very large biased sample is still biased — and more confidently wrong.

The rule for a risk analyst: big data for detection (something is happening, here, now); small, carefully coded data for measurement (how much, compared with what).



7.2.6 6. Composite indicators — the OECD/JRC discipline
A composite indicator combines several indicators into one number — country-risk ratings, governance indices, your team’s exposure index. The OECD/JRC Handbook (2008) sets out ten steps; the five that decide most of the outcome are:








Step
The choice
The risk




Theoretical framework
Which dimensions of risk, and why
An index of whatever data were available


Missing data
Drop, impute, or flag
Countries silently disappear — usually the risky ones


Normalisation
Min–max, z-score, rank, distance to a reference
Different methods, different rankings


Weighting and aggregation
Equal, statistical, expert; additive or geometric
Additive aggregation lets a strength compensate for a weakness


Sensitivity analysis
How much do results move when choices change?
A ranking presented as fact that one weight would overturn



Min–max normalisation puts every indicator on 0–1, with the direction made consistent (higher = more risk):
\[
x^{*} = \frac{x - \min x}{\max x - \min x}
\qquad\text{or, for an indicator where higher is safer,}\qquad
x^{*} = \frac{\max x - x}{\max x - \min x}
\]
Weighted additive aggregation: \(\;CI = \dfrac{\sum_j w_j\, x^{*}_j}{\sum_j w_j}\).
The point for the board. Weights are value judgements. Show them; let the reader move them; and report whether the ranking survives. A composite that hides its weights is an opinion dressed as a measurement.



7.2.7 7. The Tableau skill of the day

Tableau Prep (or the data source pane): parse a quarter string into a date; aggregate firm- quarters to quarters; union or join sources on a common key.
A highlight table of coder A × coder B, with grand totals: the agreement matrix, read straight off the screen.
Normalisation with LOD: { MIN([x]) } and { MAX([x]) } — a FIXED expression with no dimension computes over the whole table.
Parameters as weights, and RANK() to show how the ranking moves when the weights do.

The targets. (a) Hassan et al. (2019): average firm-level political risk over time, against the EPU index. (b) Your own coded index — 40 headlines, two coders, a kappa. (c) A composite exposure index for your team’s firm, with weights the board can move — your team’s draft.

Data: ../data/README.md. Provenance log as always — one line per file, including your own coding_sheet.xlsx (“produced by the team, protocol of Session 07”).


7.3.1 (a) Firm-level political risk against EPU — 30 min

7.3.1.1 Prepare — choose a route
The firm file is firm × quarter; EPU is monthly. Both must reach a common quarter grain.
The quarter identifier in the firm file is a string such as 2010q1 in the vintages we have seen — check yours. Convert it to a date:
[Quarter date] = MAKEDATE( INT(LEFT([date], 4)),
                           (INT(RIGHT([date], 1)) - 1) * 3 + 1,
                           1 )
And for EPU (Year and Month in the current file; Year may arrive as text because of the citation rows at the bottom, hence the INT):
[Quarter date] = DATETRUNC('quarter', MAKEDATE(INT([Year]), INT([Month]), 1))
Route 1 · Tableau Prep (if your licence includes it)

Input firmquarter_2022q1.csv → Clean step: add [Quarter date] → Aggregate step: group by [Quarter date]; AVG(PRisk), COUNTD([gvkey]).
Input the EPU workbook → Clean: add [Quarter date], drop rows with no value → Aggregate: group by [Quarter date]; AVG([GEPU_current]) (or GEPU_ppp — log which).
Join the two on [Quarter date] (inner) → Output as .hyper. Open it in Tableau Desktop.
Every step is a visible, saved decision: export the flow (.tfl) with your hand-in.

Route 2 · the data source pane (Tableau Desktop or Tableau Public edition)

Connect to both files. Drag the firm file to the canvas, then the EPU sheet next to it.
In the relationship dialog, choose Create Relationship Calculation on each side and enter the two [Quarter date] formulas above.
Relationships aggregate each table at its own level: AVG(PRisk) is averaged over firms, AVG(GEPU_current) over the months of the quarter — exactly what you want.



7.3.1.2 Replicate — Sheet “Firm-level political risk and EPU”

[Quarter date] → Columns as continuous Quarter.
AVG(PRisk) → Rows; the EPU measure → Rows; dual axis, not synchronised (different units).
Annotate three peaks; check what happened in those quarters.
Title with the finding; caption with both sources, vintages and access dates.



7.3.1.3 Compare

Do the two series move together? Where do they part company — and which one would you trust for a firm, and which for a country?
Add COUNTD of firms as a third view. Does the number of firms change over the period? Why does that matter for an average?
Filter hqcountrycode (2-letter codes) to exclude US. How many firms are left?





7.3.2 (b) Your coded index — 20 min
Connect to coded/coding_sheet.xlsx.

The agreement matrix. coder_A → Rows, coder_B → Columns, CNT(id) → Text and Colour: a highlight table. Analysis → Totals → Show Row and Column Grand Totals.
Percent agreement in Tableau:
[Agree] = IF [coder_A] = [coder_B] THEN 1 ELSE 0 END      →   AVG([Agree]) = p_o
Kappa, by hand. From the grand totals, compute \(p_e = \sum_k (n_{A,k}/N)(n_{B,k}/N)\) and \(\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)\). Write both on your slide. If categories are sparse, also compute kappa on three collapsed categories (0 / threat / act) — and say which you report.
Adjudicate. The adjudicator reads every disagreement and fills final, with a one-line reason. List the protocol changes you would make.
The index. From final: the share of headlines in each category, and the share coded geopolitical (≠ 0) by month. Mark econ comments separately: how many headlines about sanctions or export controls did the GPR categories force into 0?




7.3.3 (c) A composite exposure index with moving weights — 30 min

7.3.3.1 Select
Start from a spine: a sheet listing your firm’s key countries plus comparators — 8 to 12 countries, with iso3. Every input is left-joined to it, so missing values are visible rather than silently dropped.









Indicator

Direction
Preparation




Country GPR

pivot country columns; add iso3 (the columns are country names such as UK, US, Korea, and China appears three times); average the last 12 months

Each input must be one row per country before it is joined to the spine — otherwise the min and max below are taken over months, not countries. Reduce each input first: an Aggregate step in Tableau Prep, or — in Desktop — a small sheet (country × the averaged value) exported with Worksheet → Export → Crosstab into a derived file in data/derived/, logged as such. Raw files are never edited.


7.3.3.2 Normalise
Min–max across the spine countries, with a FIXED expression over the whole table:
[GPR n]   = ([GPR]   - {MIN([GPR])})   / ({MAX([GPR])}   - {MIN([GPR])})
[WGI n]   = ({MAX([WGI])} - [WGI])     / ({MAX([WGI])}   - {MIN([WGI])})      // inverted
…and the same for EPU and voting distance.


7.3.3.3 Weight
Create four parameters, w GPR, w EPU, w WGI, w Vote — integers 0 to 5, default 1 — and show their controls. Missing values must not count as zero risk, so reweight over the indicators that exist:
[Composite] =
  ( IF NOT ISNULL([GPR n])  THEN [w GPR]  * [GPR n]  ELSE 0 END
  + IF NOT ISNULL([EPU n])  THEN [w EPU]  * [EPU n]  ELSE 0 END
  + IF NOT ISNULL([WGI n])  THEN [w WGI]  * [WGI n]  ELSE 0 END
  + IF NOT ISNULL([Vote n]) THEN [w Vote] * [Vote n] ELSE 0 END )
  /
  ( IF NOT ISNULL([GPR n])  THEN [w GPR]  ELSE 0 END
  + IF NOT ISNULL([EPU n])  THEN [w EPU]  ELSE 0 END
  + IF NOT ISNULL([WGI n])  THEN [w WGI]  ELSE 0 END
  + IF NOT ISNULL([Vote n]) THEN [w Vote] ELSE 0 END )
That is a decision, not a fix: write it in your log (“composite renormalised over available indicators”).
Sheet: countries on Rows, sorted by SUM([Composite]), bars, with RANK(SUM([Composite])) as a label.


7.3.3.4 Test
Record each country’s rank under equal weights, then under each indicator alone (weight 1, others 0). In a small table: how many countries change rank by more than two places? Which country is most sensitive to the weights — and why?

text:
8.2 The lecture
The session opens with four Risk Briefs (20 min). The lecture follows.


8.2.1 1. Is cyberspace a domain of geopolitics?
Two caricatures dominate public debate. In the first, cyberspace is a revolutionary battlefield: a “cyber Pearl Harbor” can switch off a country’s grid, and small states or non-state actors can humble great powers. In the second, cyber operations are simply crime and espionage with better tools, of no strategic consequence.
Both are claims about evidence, and this session puts them to data. The question for a multinational is narrower and more practical: through which channels does inter-state rivalry in cyberspace reach my operations, and how should my decision architecture absorb it?
Three kinds of activity are easily confused:










Purpose
Typical actor
Example of the type




Espionage
Steal information — state secrets or intellectual property
intelligence services, contractors
intrusion into a defence supplier’s network


Disruption and degradation
Interrupt or damage systems
military and intelligence units, proxies
denial of service against a ministry; wiper malware


Crime
Extract money
criminal groups, sometimes tolerated or used by states
ransomware against a hospital or a pipeline operator



The boundaries blur — states tolerate, hire or shelter criminal groups — and that blurring is itself a geopolitical fact.



8.2.2 2. Valeriano and Maness: cyber war versus cyber realities
Valeriano and Maness (2015) built a dataset of cyber incidents and campaigns between rival states — pairs of states with a history of enduring hostility — and asked what the record actually shows. Their argument, in four propositions:

Restraint. States use cyber operations far less, and far less destructively, than the “cyber war” narrative predicts. The severity of most incidents is low: defacements, denial of service, espionage — rarely physical destruction.
Regional rivals. Cyber conflict mostly follows existing rivalries — the United States and China, Russia and its neighbours, Israel and Iran, India and Pakistan, the two Koreas. Cyber does not create new conflicts; it is a tool in old ones.
Why restraint? Fear of escalation and blowback, the risk of revealing and losing a capability once used, the possibility that a weapon is reverse-engineered and turned back, and the value of keeping networks intact to spy on them.
Limited coercive effect. Cyber operations rarely change the target’s behaviour. They are better at signalling and spying than at compelling.

The Dyadic Cyber Incident and Campaign Data (DCID) extends that work; version 2.0 covers 2000–2020. It is today’s replication data.
What restraint does not mean for the firm. Low strategic severity is perfectly compatible with high commercial cost. An operation that barely registers on a scale of interstate harm can still halt a company’s production for weeks.



8.2.3 3. Farrell and Newman: weaponised interdependence
Farrell and Newman (2019) look at the networks that globalisation built — finance, communications, the internet’s infrastructure — and observe that they are not flat. They have hubs. States that have jurisdiction over a hub can use it:








Effect
Mechanism
Example of the type




Panopticon
Use access to the hub to see what flows through it
intelligence access to data transiting cables, data centres or cloud providers under a state’s jurisdiction


Chokepoint
Use control of the hub to deny access to others
cutting banks out of a financial-messaging network; denying firms access to software, chips or cloud services



For a multinational, the implication is uncomfortable: the firm itself can be the hub. Its cloud, its payment rails, its software updates are infrastructure that its home state can watch or weaponise — and that rival states therefore treat as a target. This is the bridge from cyber (today) to sanctions (Session 10) and space (Session 11).



8.2.4 4. The attribution problem
Every cyber dataset rests on attribution: someone has to say who did it. Attribution is

slow — months or years after the event;
probabilistic — technical indicators can be faked or reused;
political — governments choose when to attribute publicly, and to whom;
selective — what is attributed is what someone wanted known.

So event data on cyber operations is a record of public attributions, not a record of operations. That is the most important caveat of today’s practice round — and the heart of its “catch”.



8.2.5 5. When the firm is collateral: NotPetya and its lessons
In June 2017 the NotPetya malware, spread through a Ukrainian accounting-software update and widely attributed by Western governments to Russian military intelligence, spread far beyond its apparent target. Shipping, pharmaceutical, food and logistics multinationals reported very large losses — Maersk, Merck and Mondelez among them.
Three lessons for the firm:

Proximity is technical, not political. Firms were hit because they ran a piece of software in Ukraine, not because anyone chose them.
Insurance is not a backstop. Insurers invoked war exclusions to contest claims; the litigation that followed pushed the market to write explicit exclusions for state-backed cyber operations (Lloyd’s required them from 2023). A firm’s cyber cover may end exactly where geopolitics begins.
The board owns it. Securities regulators increasingly require disclosure of material cyber incidents and of board oversight of cyber risk.




8.2.6 6. Digital sovereignty and the splintering of the network
States increasingly regulate where data sits and who may access it: data-localisation rules, restrictions on cross-border data transfers, security reviews of foreign cloud and telecoms equipment, bans on particular vendors. For a multinational this is geopolitical risk in its architecture:

Duplication costs — separate data centres or cloud regions per jurisdiction;
Conflicting obligations — one state’s law requires disclosure that another’s forbids;
Vendor risk — a supplier banned in one market may be mandatory in another.




8.2.7 7. Cyber risk in the decision architecture of the firm







Who
Role in geopolitical cyber risk




Board
Sets risk appetite; oversees disclosure; asks which state actors would want our data or our downtime?


CISO
Turns threat intelligence into controls; owns incident response


Chief risk officer
Integrates cyber with country, sanctions and supply-chain risk — the team-project view


Insurer
Prices the risk — and draws the line at state-backed operations


Regulators
Impose disclosure, localisation and vendor rules



The question to bring to the practice round: if the dataset shows where interstate cyber conflict concentrates, how should a firm with operations in those dyads change its architecture?



8.2.8 8. The Tableau skill of the day
A highlight table (rows × columns, colour = count) turns the incident list into an initiator × target matrix. A filter action on a dashboard lets a click on one cell filter the time series and the method breakdown on the other sheets. Step by step: ../02-practice/README.md.

title: 9  The redefinition of economic diplomacy
text:
9.2 The lecture
The session opens with four Risk Briefs (20 min). The lecture follows.


9.2.1 1. What economic diplomacy was, and what it has become
Economic diplomacy is the use of the instruments of foreign policy for economic ends — and of economic instruments for foreign-policy ends. In the post-1990 order (Session 02) it was mostly the first: negotiate trade agreements, open markets, promote exports, attract investment. Diplomats served firms.
Three shifts have redefined it:








Shift
What changed
Consequence for the firm




Securitisation
Trade, investment and technology are now treated as matters of national security
Firms face screening, export controls and “trusted vendor” rules from their own side


From promotion to coercion
The same networks used to promote exports are used to deny access (Session 08’s chokepoints; Session 10’s sanctions)
Home-state support can become home-state constraint overnight


Digitalisation
Diplomacy is conducted in public, on social media, aimed at domestic and foreign publics at once
Firms are drawn into public diplomatic quarrels — boycotts, hashtags, official denunciations






9.2.2 2. Putnam: two-level games
Putnam (1988) models international negotiation as two simultaneous games:

Level I — negotiators bargain with each other to reach a tentative agreement;
Level II — each negotiator’s domestic constituencies decide whether to ratify it.

The win-set is the set of Level I agreements that would be ratified at Level II. Three lessons:

Larger win-sets make agreement more likely — but leave a negotiator open to being pushed.
A small win-set is a bargaining asset: “my parliament will never accept that” is credible when it is true.
Negotiators play both boards at once: they try to shape the other side’s Level II and to manage their own.

For the firm. Multinationals are Level II actors in several countries at once. An export industry that lobbies for a trade deal enlarges the win-set at home; a firm exposed abroad may be a hostage at the other side’s Level II.



9.2.3 3. Bjola and Manor: the two-level game goes digital
Bjola and Manor (2018) revisit Putnam through the negotiations over the Iran nuclear agreement (2015). Their argument: digital diplomacy — ministries and leaders communicating directly with publics on social media — gives negotiators a new tool to act on Level II, their own and the other side’s. Governments used digital channels to build domestic support for ratification and to reach the counterpart’s public, reshaping win-sets during the negotiation itself.
Two implications for multinationals:

Speed. Domestic opinion now moves within the negotiation, not after it — so the regulatory outcome a firm plans for can change faster.
Exposure. A firm’s brand can be pulled into a digital campaign by either government.




9.2.4 4. Rose: embassies as export promotion
Rose (2007) asks whether the foreign service earns its keep. He combines the number of embassies and consulates that a set of exporting countries keep abroad with their bilateral exports, in a gravity framework that controls for the size of and distance between partners. His finding: exports are higher where a country keeps more posts, and the association survives the standard gravity controls. He reports that an additional consulate is associated with a further rise in exports of several percent — read the size off his tables, and note which kind of post matters most.
Three objections, which the practice round tests:








Objection
The worry
How to probe it




Reverse causality
Countries open posts where they already trade
Do posts predict future trade growth, or only follow past trade?


Omitted variables
Large, rich, close partners get more posts and more trade
Divide trade by partner GDP; colour by distance or region


Measurement
A post is not a budget; an honorary consulate is not an embassy
Separate embassies from consulates



Rose takes reverse causality seriously and argues that the evidence is consistent with posts having an effect, but a cross-section cannot settle it. That is the catch of the day.



9.2.5 5. The firm and the state: bargaining, screening, and diplomacy by firms
Triangular diplomacy. Stopford and Strange (1991) argued that diplomacy is no longer only state–state: it is also state–firm (governments bargain with multinationals over investment) and firm–firm (alliances). Vernon’s obsolescing bargain (1971) adds the dynamic: once a firm’s capital is sunk, its bargaining power falls.
Investment screening is economic diplomacy aimed at firms: the US Committee on Foreign Investment (CFIUS), the EU framework regulation on FDI screening (Regulation 2019/452), and the national-security review under the Investment Canada Act. Screening has widened from defence to data, critical minerals, infrastructure and technology.
Commercial diplomacy — the toolbox:







Instrument
Example of the type




Embassies and consulates
trade commissioners, market intelligence, introductions


Trade missions and state visits
ministers travelling with business delegations


Export credit and insurance
export credit agencies covering political risk


Investment promotion agencies
incentives, aftercare


Treaties
investment treaties with dispute settlement



When to lean on the home state — and when that is itself a risk: in a dispute, home-state backing helps; in a confrontation between states, being seen as an instrument of one may make the firm a target of the other.



9.2.6 6. The Tableau skill of the day
A log scale (Edit Axis → Logarithmic) for variables that span orders of magnitude; a trend line (Analytics → Trend Line) and Describe Trend Model for its R² and p-value. Neither tells you the direction of causation. Step by step: ../02-practice/README.md.

title: 10  Economic sanctions
text:
10.2 The lecture
The session opens with Quiz 3 (20 min) and four Risk Briefs (20 min). The lecture is therefore shorter today.


10.2.1 1. The instrument of first resort
Economic sanctions are restrictions on economic relations imposed by one or more senders on a target — a state, a government, a firm or an individual — to change its behaviour, weaken it, or signal disapproval. Their use has grown markedly since the end of the Cold War; the Global Sanctions Data Base documents the rise and its changing composition.







Dimension
Categories




Sender
unilateral (one state) · plurilateral (the EU, a coalition) · multilateral (the UN Security Council)


Type
trade · financial · travel · arms · military assistance · other — the GSDB’s classification


Scope
comprehensive (a whole economy) vs targeted or “smart” (named persons, firms, sectors)


Objective
change a policy · destabilise a regime · end a war or a territorial conflict · prevent war · fight terrorism · human rights · democracy






10.2.2 2. Do they work? The great debate
Hufbauer, Schott, Elliott and Oegg (2007) — the third edition of a study first published in 1985 — code each episode on two components: how far the policy outcome sought was achieved, and how far sanctions contributed to it. Combining the two, they judge roughly a third of cases at least partly successful, with success more likely when goals are modest, the target is small, weak and friendly to the sender, and sanctions are imposed quickly and decisively.
Pape (1997) re-examined the cases counted as successes and argued that most do not survive scrutiny: in many, the outcome was achieved by force, was not really conceded, or cannot be attributed to sanctions. His conclusion: economic sanctions rarely achieve major political goals. Elliott (1998) replied that the glass is half full rather than empty — the debate turns on coding.
The selection effect (Drezner, 2003). If targets that would concede do so when sanctions are only threatened, then the cases we observe as imposed are the hard ones. Imposed sanctions will look ineffective even if the instrument works. This is why TIES records threats as well as impositions — and why the practice round compares the two.

The lesson for an analyst. “Do sanctions work?” has no answer independent of how a case, an objective and a success are coded. Every number in this debate is a coding decision.




10.2.3 3. From comprehensive to smart sanctions
The humanitarian cost of the comprehensive sanctions on Iraq in the 1990s pushed senders towards targeted measures: asset freezes and travel bans on named individuals, sectoral restrictions, financial measures. Farrell and Newman (Session 08) explain why financial sanctions became the weapon of choice: the dollar-clearing system and financial-messaging networks are chokepoints under the jurisdiction of a few senders.
Targeted does not mean contained. Sanctions on banks, insurers and shippers propagate to every firm that depends on them.



10.2.4 4. The firm in the middle
The compliance perimeter. A firm must screen customers, suppliers, banks and vessels against sanctions lists — in the US, the Treasury’s OFAC lists; in the EU, Council regulations; in Canada, regulations under the Special Economic Measures Act and related statutes. Ownership rules extend listings to entities owned by listed persons, so the perimeter is wider than the list.
Secondary sanctions threaten third-country firms with penalties — loss of access to the sender’s market or financial system — for dealing with the target. They make a sender’s foreign policy binding on firms that are not its nationals.
Overcompliance and de-risking. Because penalties are severe and the rules complex, banks and firms often withdraw from whole markets or sectors the law does not close. The effective scope of sanctions is set by compliance departments as much as by governments.
The exit decision: Russia 2022. Following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Western sanctions and public pressure led many multinationals to suspend, scale back or leave Russian operations. Exits were complicated by countermeasures — approval requirements and discounts on sales of foreign assets, and in some cases temporary state management of foreign-owned firms. The firm’s options:








Option
Cost
Risk




Stay
reputational, compliance burden
new sanctions; asset seizure; home-state pressure


Suspend
idle assets
write-off if the situation persists


Sell
forced discount, approval delays
buyer later sanctioned; buy-back clauses


Walk away
full write-off
—






10.2.5 5. What a risk dashboard should track

Exposure — the firm’s revenues, assets and suppliers in sanctioned or at-risk jurisdictions;
Pipeline — threats and announced measures (the TIES lesson);
Propagation — banks, insurers, logistics providers whose own exposure would cut the firm off;
Counter-measures — what the target can do to foreign firms on its soil.




10.2.6 6. The Tableau skill of the day
A year scaffold joined with a range condition (Year ≥ begin_year and Year ≤ end_year, in the GSDB’s column names) turns episodes into active cases per year; a Gantt chart draws each episode as a bar from start to end. Step by step: ../02-practice/README.md.
