title: 11  Space geopolitics
text:
11.2 The lecture
The session opens with four Risk Briefs (20 min). The lecture follows.


11.2.1 1. Infrastructure in orbit
Few multinationals own a satellite. Almost all of them depend on one. Three services carry most of that dependence:








Service
What the firm uses it for
Who provides it




Positioning, navigation and timing (PNT)
fleet and container tracking, aviation and shipping, precision agriculture — and above all time: telecom networks, power grids and trading venues synchronise their clocks to GNSS signals
four global systems, each run by a state: GPS (United States), Galileo (European Union), BeiDou (China), GLONASS (Russia)


Connectivity
ships, aircraft, mines, rigs and remote sites; back-up links for networks on the ground
geostationary operators, and since 2019 constellations of thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit


Earth observation
crop and commodity forecasts, insurance claims, supply-chain and site monitoring, due diligence
state agencies and a growing number of commercial imaging firms



Sessions 08 and 10 showed how networks become instruments of power. Today’s network is physically above the firm, and its hubs are a handful of states and, increasingly, a handful of companies. The scale of the change is recent: ESA’s 2026 report notes that the exponential growth in the number of new payloads continued in 2025, driven by a higher launch frequency, rideshare launches and the deployment of large constellations by commercial operators (ESA Space Debris Office, 2026).



11.2.2 2. The orbital commons: law and physics
The law. The Outer Space Treaty (1967) is the constitution of the domain, and it was written for two superpowers, not for a market:








Article
Rule
What it means for a firm




II
outer space “is not subject to national appropriation” by claim of sovereignty, use or occupation
no one can own an orbit — but whoever occupies it first, in practice, keeps it


IV
no nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit; the Moon and celestial bodies for peaceful purposes only
conventional weapons in orbit and anti-satellite tests are not prohibited by the Treaty


VI
states bear international responsibility for national activities, “whether … carried on by governmental agencies or by non-governmental entities”, which require “authorization and continuing supervision”
every commercial satellite has a state behind it — its licensing state


VII
the launching state is liable for damage caused by its objects
debris has an owner, in law, long after it has stopped working


IX
“due regard” to the interests of others; consultations before potentially harmful interference
the closest the Treaty comes to traffic rules — without an enforcer



Two further layers matter to business. The International Telecommunication Union coordinates radio frequencies and orbital positions through its Radio Regulations: an operator’s state files a satellite network with the ITU and coordinates it with earlier filings, so priority goes, broadly, to the first to file — an incentive to file early and large, sometimes for “paper satellites” that may never fly. And national licensing — of launches, spectrum, remote sensing, exports — is where the Treaty’s “authorization and continuing supervision” becomes a permit a firm must hold.
The physics. Kessler and Cour-Palais (1978) showed that once the density of objects in an orbital shell passes a threshold, collisions produce fragments that cause further collisions: a debris belt that grows on its own, even if no one launches again. A commons in the strict sense — no one can be excluded, and every use depletes it for others — with physics in place of an economy. Debris in low orbit re-enters as the atmosphere drags it down; the higher the orbit, the longer it stays — years at a few hundred kilometres, decades to centuries above that.

For the firm: an orbit is a shared infrastructure whose quality is set by the least careful actor in it. A destructive test by one state raises the collision risk — and the insurance price — of every operator in that shell.




11.2.3 3. Astropolitics: three readings of the new space race









Reading
Implication




Dolman (2002), Astropolitik
classical geopolitics carried into space: in the spirit of Mackinder, whoever controls low Earth orbit controls access to near-Earth space, and through it the Earth; a realist case for the United States to take and hold that control
space is a territory to dominate — Session 03’s anarchy, with orbits as chokepoints


Pekkanen (2019), “Governing the new space race”
the new space race is driven by three intertwined trends — democratisation (more states and non-state actors), commercialisation (firms striking out on their own, not only supplying governments), militarisation — while about 95% of space technologies are dual-use, and treaty-making is in decline
space is a market governed by national laws, contracts and a few old principles — and the firms in it are part of the security problem


Bowen (2020), War in Space
spacepower matters for its effects on Earth; Earth orbit is a “cosmic coastline” from which states support, and threaten, what happens on land, at sea and in the air
space is infrastructure for terrestrial power — and therefore a target when terrestrial power is contested



The three readings do not exclude one another. Read together they explain why the same constellation can be a consumer broadband business, a military communications network and a foreign-policy instrument, all at once — Pekkanen’s dual use, with the strategic stakes of Dolman and Bowen.



11.2.4 4. Counterspace: the threats
The Secure World Foundation’s annual open-source assessment (Samson & Brett, 2026) tracks what states can do to deceive, disrupt, deny, degrade or destroy space systems, across five categories, in thirteen countries:









Category
What it is
Reversible?
Who it hits first




Direct-ascent
a missile launched from Earth to destroy a satellite
no — and it creates debris
the target, then every operator in that shell


Co-orbital
a satellite that approaches, inspects, interferes with or attacks another
depends
the target


Electronic warfare
jamming or spoofing of signals — uplinks, downlinks, GNSS
yes
users on the ground: ships, aircraft, networks


Directed energy
lasers or microwaves to dazzle or damage sensors
partly
imaging satellites


Cyber
attacks on satellites, ground stations or user terminals
yes, unless hardware is destroyed
customers of the operator



Its central finding for this course: many states have researched and tested destructive capabilities, but only non-destructive capabilities are actively used against satellites in current military operations. Four states have destroyed a satellite with a missile from the ground: the United States (1985, and the low-altitude intercept of a failing satellite in 2008), China (2007), India (2019) and Russia (2021). In April 2022 the United States declared it would not conduct destructive direct-ascent tests, and the UN General Assembly called on all states to make the same commitment in December 2022.
What firms have actually suffered is the reversible kind. On 24 February 2022, the day of the invasion of Ukraine, a cyberattack on the ground segment of Viasat’s KA-SAT network disabled thousands of user modems in Ukraine and across Europe — including the remote monitoring of thousands of wind turbines in Germany; the EU, the UK and the US attributed it to Russia. GNSS jamming and spoofing around conflict zones has become routine; in 2024 Finnair suspended flights to Tartu, in Estonia, for several weeks because interference made satellite-based approaches unusable.

The lesson for an analyst. Destructive tests make headlines and debris. Jamming, spoofing and cyberattacks on ground segments make losses — and they fall on the customers, not on the satellite.




11.2.5 5. The evidence: the debris record
ESA’s Space Debris Office has published its Space Environment Report every year since 2017. The 2026 edition (Issue 10.0, data to the end of 2025) is today’s big work. Its method is worth reading before its figures: it counts catalogued objects — from the US public catalogue, the Russian Vimpel catalogue and the UK’s historical RAE tables — and asserted objects known to exist by design, cross-correlated in ESA’s DISCOS database; objects too small or too erratic to be tracked are outside its scope.
Its headline numbers, at the end of 2025 (Table 3.1):

44,964 objects in Earth orbit, of which 16,946 payloads; 25,060 in low Earth orbit;
“ever since the start of the space age there has been more space debris in orbit than operational satellites”;
fragmentations other than collisions — explosions, mostly of old rocket stages and batteries — are the dominant source of debris: on average 9.8 non-deliberate fragmentations a year over the last two decades; 2024 added over 3,000 catalogued fragments, mostly from propulsion-related break-ups.

The target figure — Figure 2.1, the number of objects in geocentric orbit by object class since 1957 — shows the cumulative result. Three events stand out, all recorded in the report:









Date
Event
Altitude
What it did




11 January 2007
China destroys its Fengyun-1C weather satellite with a ground-launched missile
about 850 km
the largest single source of catalogued debris in the public catalogue; thousands of fragments, most still in orbit


10 February 2009
the active Iridium 33 and the defunct Cosmos 2251 collide
about 780 km
the first accidental collision between two intact satellites — Kessler, observed


15 November 2021
Russia destroys Cosmos 1408 with a ground-launched missile
about 470–490 km
some 1,800 catalogued fragments; low enough that almost all re-entered within three years — ESA attributes the 2022 spike in re-entering debris to the test



What the figure does not measure. It counts objects, not risk: a 10-cm fragment and a 5-tonne rocket stage each count once, and objects too small to catalogue — the majority of the fragments able to disable a satellite — do not appear at all. And it is drawn from catalogues that themselves improve: when sensors get better, the number of objects rises without anything new happening in orbit. In the practice round, you will find a third limit — the one hidden in how the public catalogue dates debris.



11.2.6 6. One operator: concentration, and weaponised interdependence in orbit
The new space race has a feature the Cold War one did not: most of the active satellites in orbit belong to one company. SpaceX’s Starlink, first launched in May 2019, grew in six years into the majority of the world’s operating satellites; you will measure how large a majority in the practice round, and you will find that concentration of who launches payloads has returned to Cold War levels — with a firm, not a superpower, at the top.
Starlink in Ukraine shows what that means. Within days of the 2022 invasion, Starlink terminals became a backbone of Ukraine’s military and civil communications. The company’s own decisions about where the service would work — including, by its owner’s account, a refusal to enable it for an attack near Crimea in 2022 — became questions of war policy, and governments moved to contract for the service directly.
Read it with Farrell and Newman (2019) from Session 08. A constellation is a hub: its operator sees who connects, where (a panopticon), and can switch a user, a region or a country off (a chokepoint). The two conditions for weaponisation are met when the network is concentrated and when a state can direct the firm that runs the hub — and Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty guarantees that every operator has a licensing state behind it. A firm that depends on one operator depends on that operator’s state as well.
States are responding as you would expect from Session 03: by building their own. The EU’s IRIS² secure-connectivity programme (Regulation (EU) 2023/588), China’s Qianfan and Guowang constellations, and national launch programmes are all, in part, answers to dependence on one American firm. Export controls draw the same line from the other side: spacecraft and their components sit on the US Munitions List (Category XV of the ITAR) or, for most commercial satellites since 2014, under the Export Administration Regulations (the “9x515” entries) — so a non-US manufacturer with a US component needs US permission to sell to some customers.



11.2.7 7. What can the firm do?
Through which channel does space risk reach the P&L? The course’s five channels apply:








Channel

What a dashboard should track — each with a threshold that triggers a named decision:

Dependence — the share of a critical service (connectivity, imagery, timing) supplied by one operator or one state’s system; e.g. above 50% from one operator → contract a second one.
Interference — official warnings of GNSS interference (aviation authorities publish them) in the regions where the firm’s ships, aircraft or sites operate.
Environment — destructive tests and fragmentation events in the orbital shells of the firm’s providers; ESA’s yearly environment indicators.
Rules — changes in export-control lists, licensing conditions and ITU filings that affect the firm’s suppliers or markets.

11.2.8 8. The Tableau skill of the day

A stock from flows. Pivot LAUNCH_DATE and DECAY_DATE into one Event date column; a calculated field Change = +1 for a launch, −1 for a decay; SUM([Change]) by year with a Running Total table calculation is the number of objects in orbit.
HHI with LOD expressions. Share of each owner in a year’s payloads: {FIXED [Launch year], [OWNER] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])} / {FIXED [Launch year] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])}; the sum of squared shares, built so that it adds up correctly over rows, is the HHI.
Dashboard action across data sources: Dashboard → Actions → Add Action → Filter, mapping Year in one source to Launch year in the other.

title: 11  Space geopolitics
text:
11.3 In the practice

The target. ESA’s Space Environment Report 2026, Figure 2.1: the number of objects in geocentric orbit by object class, from 1957 to the end of 2025, with the 2007 Chinese ASAT test, the 2009 Iridium–Cosmos collision and the 2021 Russian ASAT test annotated — rebuilt from the public catalogue. You add the concentration of who puts payloads into orbit, year by year, and who operates the active satellites today — and wire the views into one dashboard with an action.

The last practice round of the term. The last twenty minutes of Session 10 reviewed your team dashboard’s skeleton. Most skeletons still lack a space-infrastructure channel and any interaction between views. Leave today with both: the dependence view you build is designed to be dropped into your team dashboard, for the satellite services your own firm relies on.
Work in your project teams. Everyone builds the workbook; the team hands in one.


11.3.1 1 · Collect — 15 min
You arrive with satcat.csv (one download per team, pre-session). Use these fifteen minutes to check, not to download again:

The snapshot. What is the latest LAUNCH_DATE in the file? Log it with your download date: the catalogue changes every day.
The codes. Open the format documentation and the status codes. Which OBJECT_TYPE values are present? Which OPS_STATUS_CODE values count as active? What does a blank status mean?
The trap you found before class. Filter OBJECT_NAME = FENGYUN 1C DEB. How many rows? Which LAUNCH_DATE? Write the gap to 11 January 2007 in your log.

Provenance log — one line per file, as always:

11.3.2 2 · Prepare — 15 min
You build two data sources from the same file: one reshaped into events (for the stock of objects in orbit), one left as it is (for concentration).

11.3.2.1 Data source A · “SATCAT events”

Connect → Text file → satcat.csv. Check the types: LAUNCH_DATE and DECAY_DATE must be dates (click the type icon above the column if they arrive as strings), NORAD_CAT_ID a number.
Data source filter (top right of the data source page → Filters → Add): ORBIT_CENTER = EA. Objects around the Sun or the Moon never decay and would stay “in orbit” for ever.
Pivot the two dates. Select LAUNCH_DATE and DECAY_DATE in the grid → right-click → Pivot. Rename Pivot Field Names → Event and Pivot Field Values → Event date. Each object now has two rows: its launch and its decay (empty if it is still in space).
Calculated fields:
Change  =  IF [Event] = "LAUNCH_DATE" THEN 1 ELSE -1 END
Year    =  YEAR([Event date])
Check the grain. Note the row count before and after the pivot, then exclude the null Event date rows (decays that have not happened). What is one row now? Write it in the log.



11.3.2.2 Data source B · “SATCAT objects”

Data → New Data Source → the same satcat.csv, not pivoted. Data source filter OBJECT_TYPE = PAY — a data source filter, not a sheet filter (step 3 explains why).
Calculated fields:
Launch year  =  YEAR([LAUNCH_DATE])
Power        =  CASE [OWNER] WHEN "US" THEN "United States"
                             WHEN "PRC" THEN "China"
                             WHEN "CIS" THEN "USSR / Russia"
                             ELSE "Rest of the world" END
Active       =  [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "+" OR [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "P" OR [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "B"
                OR [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "S" OR [OPS_STATUS_CODE] = "X"
Operator     =  IF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "STARLINK") THEN "Starlink (SpaceX)"
                ELSEIF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "ONEWEB") THEN "OneWeb"
                ELSEIF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "KUIPER") THEN "Kuiper (Amazon)"
                ELSEIF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "QIANFAN") THEN "Qianfan"
                ELSEIF STARTSWITH([OBJECT_NAME], "HULIANWANG") THEN "Guowang"
                ELSE "Other: " + [OWNER] END
CIS is CelesTrak’s code for the USSR and Russia; OWNER is a registry-style code, not the operator — log both decisions.





11.3.3 3 · Replicate — 35 min

11.3.3.1 Sheet 1 · “Objects in Earth orbit, by type” — the target figure (data source A)

Year → Columns: right-click → Convert to Dimension, keep it continuous (green).
SUM([Change]) → Rows. You see net additions per year — a jagged line.
Right-click the pill → Quick Table Calculation → Running Total. Now you see the stock.
OBJECT_TYPE → Colour. Edit Table Calculation → Compute using → Specific Dimensions → tick Year only, so the running total restarts for each type. Mark type Area (stacked).
Filter Year ≤ 2025 to match ESA’s end point. Never filter out early years with a normal filter: it runs before the table calculation and the running total would restart from zero. (To hide early years, use a table-calculation filter such as LOOKUP(MIN([Year]), 0).)
Annotate 2007, 2009 and 2021 (right-click → Annotate → Point). Look at the debris band. Where are the steps?
Title stating the finding; caption with source, snapshot date and “objects dated by launch date”.



11.3.3.2 Sheet 2 · “Payloads launched per year, by power” (data source B)

Launch year → Columns (continuous dimension), CNT([NORAD_CAT_ID]) → Rows, Power → Colour, mark type Bar. Where does the Cold War end, and where does the new race begin?



11.3.3.3 Sheet 3 · “How concentrated is the new space race?” — the HHI (data source B)

Create:
Owner share  =  {FIXED [Launch year], [OWNER] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])}
              / {FIXED [Launch year] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])}
HHI piece    =  10000 * [Owner share] / {FIXED [Launch year] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])}
Why the second line: each owner’s squared share must be counted once, but the owner appears on as many rows as it has payloads. Spreading share × 10,000 over the year’s rows means that summing an owner’s rows gives exactly share² × 10,000.
Launch year → Columns, SUM([HHI piece]) → Rows, mark type Line. That sum is the HHI. Check: 1957 must give 10,000 (two Soviet payloads). Reference lines at 2,500 and 1,800, labelled.
Why the data source filter in step 6: a FIXED expression is computed before ordinary filters. Had you filtered OBJECT_TYPE on the sheet, the shares would still include debris and rocket bodies. (Adding the filter to context also works.)



11.3.3.4 Sheet 4 · “Who launched that year?” (data source B)

OWNER → Rows, CNT([NORAD_CAT_ID]) → Columns, sorted descending, Operator → Colour; a Top 10 by count filter on OWNER. This is the target of the action.



11.3.3.5 Sheet 5 · “Who operates the active satellites today?” (data source B)

Filter Active = True and ORBIT_CENTER = EA. Operator → Rows, CNT([NORAD_CAT_ID]) → Columns, sorted; Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total. Caption: “status as of the snapshot date; blank status excluded”.



11.3.3.6 Dashboard · “Space infrastructure exposure”

New Dashboard. Sheet 1 top left, Sheet 3 top right, Sheet 4 bottom left, Sheet 5 bottom right.
Action 1. Dashboard → Actions → Add Action → Filter. Source: Sheet 1. Target: Sheet 4. Run on: Select. Clearing the selection: Show all values. Filter: Selected fields → source field Year → target data source SATCAT objects, target field Launch year. Because the two sheets use different data sources, map the fields explicitly.
Action 2. The same, with Sheet 3 as source (same data source as Sheet 4: field Launch year → Launch year).
Click 1965 on Sheet 3, then 2025. Sheet 4 should show who launched that year. If it shows nothing, the field mapping is wrong: fix it, and log it.





11.3.4 4 · Compare and break — 15 min

Differ. Put Sheet 1 beside ESA’s Figure 2.1 and Table 3.1 (end of 2025: 44,964 objects, of which 16,946 payloads). Give your totals by type and one reason for each gap — which catalogues ESA adds, what it calls “unidentified”, what the public catalogue leaves out.
Break: when does debris appear? Your debris band does not step up in 2007, 2009 or 2021. Re-date the four big events’ debris to the date the event happened. In data source A:
Appearance year  =  IF [Event] = "LAUNCH_DATE" AND CONTAINS([OBJECT_NAME], "FENGYUN 1C DEB") THEN 2007
                    ELSEIF [Event] = "LAUNCH_DATE" AND (CONTAINS([OBJECT_NAME], "COSMOS 2251 DEB")
                         OR CONTAINS([OBJECT_NAME], "IRIDIUM 33 DEB")) THEN 2009
                    ELSEIF [Event] = "LAUNCH_DATE" AND CONTAINS([OBJECT_NAME], "COSMOS 1408 DEB") THEN 2021
                    ELSE [Year] END
Duplicate Sheet 1 and replace Year by Appearance year. How big is each step now? What about the thousands of other fragments whose event you did not re-date?
Break: flag or firm? On Sheet 5, replace Operator by OWNER, and compute the HHI of active satellites both ways. Which number describes your firm’s dependence better?
Extend. For your team’s firm, name the satellite services it relies on (GNSS timing, connectivity at sea or in remote sites, imagery). Find their operators in the file — NAVSTAR (GPS), GSAT0… (Galileo, coded ESA), BEIDOU, [GLONASS-M] — and add the one that matters to Sheet 5. Optional, with GCAT: orbital launch attempts per year (LaunchCode starting O or D) by launch-provider state.




11.3.5 5 · The catch — 10 min
One slide, three panels:








Original
Ours
The catch




ESA’s Figure 2.1
Your dashboard
What it does not license your firm to conclude



The model catch, if you need one to beat: a count of objects is not a count of risk — the fragments able to disable a satellite are mostly too small to catalogue, and the public catalogue dates debris by its parent’s launch, so the ASAT tests vanish from a chart built naively on it; and concentration by flag hides dependence on one firm. Beat it — say something specific to your firm.
A member drawn at random presents in two minutes.



11.3.6 Hand in
Upload to ZoneCours before leaving: the .twbx, the provenance log, and the slide. Formative: commented, not marked; counts towards participation. (The SATCAT is freely available, so the workbook may also go to Tableau Public — credit CelesTrak in the caption.)
The one rule: the log records at least one place where the data disagreed with the paper — a total that does not reach ESA’s, debris dated to the wrong year, an owner code that is not the operator.



11.3.7 Into the team dashboard
Before Session 12, re-point Sheet 5 at your firm’s satellite services, keep the action, and add the dependence view to your channel views with a threshold — for example more than half of a critical service from one operator → contract a second one. A board member should be able to click a year and see who controlled access to orbit then, and see in one screen who the firm depends on now.



11.3.8 What loses credit

A running total that restarts because early years were filtered out
Objects around the Sun or the Moon counted as “in orbit”
An HHI that is not 10,000 in 1957 — shares computed after a sheet filter, or squared on every row
OWNER presented as the operator, or blank status counted as inactive
A dashboard action that silently filters to nothing
A catch about ESA rather than about your firm

section: 12.4 The closing address — from indicators to decisions
text:
12.4 The closing address — from indicators to decisions
Ten minutes, after the last team. Its content is in the deck; in summary:

Kobrin (1979) was right about the hard part. Political risk is not the event — it is the contingency that the event affects this firm’s operations. Every dashboard presented today is a claim about that contingency.
Henisz (2000) on constraint. The POLCON index measures how many independent veto players constrain a government. Low constraint means policy can change fast — in either direction. It is the structural complement to every event- and text-based indicator of the course.
Indicators do not decide. A watchlist is useful only if each indicator has a threshold and an owner. The best dashboards today were the ones that would make someone do something on a given Monday.
What the twelve weeks established. Geopolitical risk is measured through families of indicators that disagree; each figure in a famous work is a stack of decisions; and the analyst’s job is to make those decisions visible to the person who must act.

text:
A.2 Why replicate figures, not regressions
This is not an econometrics course. The figure at the heart of a big work is where its argument meets the reader — the image that ends up in board presentations and ministerial speeches. Rebuilding it forces every decision the authors made into the open: which countries, which years, which deflator, which coding rule, which normalisation. A multinational’s risk team makes the same decisions every time it builds a dashboard. Learning to see them is the point.

title: Appendix B — Data sources
text:
B.2 Traps, source by source







Dataset
The trap




GPR
Revised monthly; vintages exist (data_gpr_export_YYYYMM.xls). Country indices are the anglophone press’s attention to a country, not that country’s risk.


WDI
Aggregates (“World”, “High income”, “G7” is not provided — build it) sit in the same file as countries. Current-dollar shares move with exchange rates.


NMC
Uses COW country codes, not ISO; states enter and exit the system (GMY absent 1946–1990, when GFR/GDR cover 1955/1954–1990). Missing components are coded -9. Yearly CINC sums run 1.000–1.075, not exactly 1. Ends in 2022.


SIPRI
Several sheets (Constant (2024) US$, Current US$, Share of GDP, Per capita, Share of Govt. spending, local-currency and Regional totals); ... = data unavailable, xxx = the state did not exist — notes atop each sheet, plus a Footnotes sheet. Country strings: United States of America; Russia from 1992, USSR before.


UNGA ideal points
Carries both COW ccode and ISO iso3c; estimated by calendar year since the July 2025 releases (v36/37; current v39, 30 July 2026) — earlier versions by session, so the variable meaning changed between versions. Higher = closer to the US.


IMF IMTS
Exports reported by A ≠ imports reported by B (“mirror” asymmetry). Choose one side and say which.


UNSC members
Two-year terms starting 1 January; election happens the October before — the paper’s “election year” matters.


US aid
Obligations vs disbursements; current vs constant dollars; the official site moved in 2025.


ISO Survey
Coverage of certification bodies changed over time: jumps in a country’s count can be reporting, not adoption.


Firm-level risk
Listed firms holding earnings calls in English — mostly US. Stops in 2021.


DCID
State-to-state rivals only; StateA/StateB are the dyad as names, not initiator and target — derive the target from initiator (COW code) and Dyadpair; coded from open sources — attribution is by definition uncertain.


EuRepoC
Much wider than DCID (includes criminal and non-state); filter on initiator_category (State / State affiliated actor) before comparing.


Lowy GDI
66 countries or territories only (including Taiwan and the EU’s EEAS); names, not codes, with typos (Portual, Nigaragua); counts posts, not staff or budget.


GSDB
Licence forbids redistribution: workbooks go to ZoneCours, never Tableau Public with the raw data. “Success” is the coders’ judgement of objectives met.


TIES
Includes threats of sanctions — a case may never have been imposed.


POLCON / WGI
WGI’s 2025 edition changed scale and recalculated history: never mix editions.


SATCAT
Debris carries its parent’s LAUNCH_DATE (Fengyun-1C debris is dated 1999, not 2007); OWNER is not the operator (Starlink US, Galileo ESA, Russia CIS); filter ORBIT_CENTER = EA; a blank status is not “inactive”; one download per team.


GCAT
The state is the launch provider’s, not the customer’s (Rocket Lab = New Zealand); vague-date text, padded values.


UCS Satellite Database
Frozen: data current through 1 May 2023. Use SATCAT for anything later.

B.3 Country codes
Join on ISO 3166 alpha-3 codes, never on names. NMC and DCID (in initiator and Dyadpair) use Correlates of War codes (official list): keep a concordance sheet (COW ccode ↔︎ ISO3) in your workbook. The countrycode concordance tables published by Arel-Bundock et al. are the standard reference. The UNGA ideal points carry iso3c too. Kosovo is KOS at the IMF and XKX at the World Bank; the West Bank and Gaza is WBG at the IMF.

C.3 3. Conventions every chart follows

A title that states the finding, not the variable. “The G7’s share of world GDP fell by a third after 1990”, not “GDP share”.
A source caption: dataset, producer, version, access date. No caption, no credit.
Units on every axis. Current US dollars or constant? Index base year? Share or count?
Direct labels in place of legends wherever there are fewer than six series.
One accent colour for the series the argument is about; greys for the rest.
Annotate the events that explain the shape of the line.
Name your decisions in a footnote: countries dropped, years rebased, codes changed.

Trap
Symptom
Fix




Joining on country names
Côte d’Ivoire, Türkiye, Korea, Rep. silently drop out

66 columns called 1960 … 2025

SUM of an index
A line ten times too high
An index is averaged, not summed. Check the aggregation on every pill

A bar for “May” across all years
Use the continuous date (green pill) for time series


Duplicated rows after a join
Totals inflate
Check the row count before and after; use a relationship instead of a join when the grain differs

Your numbers do not match last year’s paper
That is a finding, not an error: log the release you used


Aggregates in country lists
“World”, “High income” and “Euro area” counted as countries
Filter on a country list, not on “everything that is not blank”

E.4.3 Specimen answers (Part A)

Risk: probabilities estimable from experience (piracy losses on a shipping route). Uncertainty: probabilities not estimable (whether a given strait will be blockaded within five years).
Macro risk affects all foreign firms in a country (a general expropriation, currency inconvertibility); micro risk affects one sector or firm (a mining-code change, a contract cancellation).
Because newspapers’ total output changes over time; the share removes the effect of size, so the index measures relative attention to geopolitical tension.
The absence of a government above states — no authority to enforce agreements. It does not mean chaos or constant war.
